_what_this_is: The entry gate, answered BEFORE drafting. The threshold question is whether a well-informed non-expert would confidently believe something the primary sources do not support.

belief._note: What the reader already believes, stated as they would state it. If you cannot write this sentence, there is nothing to correct and no subject -- which is how the tobacco-analogy candidate died.
belief.statement: Inclusive education programmes in poorer countries help disabled children get into school and learn. The best approaches are training mainstream teachers in inclusive methods, providing assistive devices like glasses, hearing aids and wheelchairs, and making school buildings accessible. Putting children in ordinary classrooms works better than separate special schools.
belief.how_we_know_they_believe_it: The coverage that settled it. Named outlets, quoted headlines. Not 'it is widely assumed'.

what_the_sources_show._note: What the primary sources actually support, and which sources.

direction._note: CORRECTS, CONFIRMS or NARROWS. This field exists so the contrarianism guard can count. A publication whose answer is always CORRECTS is performing scepticism rather than assessing evidence, and is not to be trusted.

reader_with_a_decision: Education ministry officials, donor agencies (e.g. UNICEF, World Bank, FCDO, USAID successors) and NGO programme managers. They must decide which disability-inclusive education interventions to fund, scale or drop: teacher training, assistive technology, community-based rehabilitation, cash transfers, school accessibility upgrades, or special/resource-unit provision.

public_record_check._note: NOT 'has anybody published this'. On any contested question, somebody has. The question is whether it has been carried WHERE THIS READER WOULD FIND IT. Run the counterexample hunter on the belief statement, not on the finding.
public_record_check.our_contribution: translation, extension, or correction of the prior art -- say which

kill_condition: Systematic reviews and trials from low- and middle-income countries consistently show, with moderate or high certainty, that these programme types (teacher training, assistive devices, accessibility, inclusive placement) improve enrolment, attendance and measured learning for children with disabilities, with a clear ranking that matches the common belief.

kill_condition_tested._note: Filled in AFTER going to look, by whoever looked.

scope._note: What the answer will and will not cover, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened, so scope cannot be fitted to the findings afterwards. An omission ruled OUT_OF_SCOPE, and a headline conclusion declared out of scope, must name the question's words or one of these entries (fix 2, docs/whu-fix2-omission-rulings-design.md section 2.4).
scope.covers: Evaluated interventions in low- and middle-income countries aimed at improving educational access, participation, retention or learning outcomes for children and young people (roughly school age through youth) with any type of disability. It also covers the comparative effectiveness of different intervention types.

out.what: Effectiveness of inclusive or special education programmes in high-income countries
out.why: Different school systems, resources and evidence base. Findings do not transfer directly to the question asked.

out.what: Whether inclusion is a right or moral obligation regardless of measured effect
out.why: This is a normative and legal question (e.g. CRPD Article 24), not an empirical one about whether programmes work.

out.what: How many disabled children are out of school, and why
out.why: Prevalence and barrier descriptions set context but do not tell us whether interventions work.

out.what: Purely medical or rehabilitative interventions with no education outcome measured
out.why: The question is about education outcomes. Health effects alone do not answer it.

out.what: Cost-effectiveness and value for money of each programme type
out.why: This needs separate cost data that is rarely reported. The page will judge effectiveness only and note where cost evidence is absent.

out.what: Adult education, tertiary study and vocational or employment programmes for adults with disabilities
out.why: These fall outside 'children and young people' and the schooling outcomes in question.

evidence_standard._note: What kinds of evidence the answer will weigh, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened (post-study fix 3, docs/whu-fix3-evidence-standard.md). 'measured': outcomes measured in trials, cohorts, evaluations. 'assessed': expert assessments -- systematic-review conclusions, IPCC confidence-rated statements, guideline recommendations. When they differ, the page states both and drops neither.
evidence_standard.measured: Quantified outcomes from randomised trials, quasi-experimental and controlled before-after studies in LMICs, with effect sizes and confidence intervals. Outcomes include enrolment, attendance, dropout and completion rates, standardised learning or test scores, and validated participation measures for children with disabilities compared with a control or comparison group.
evidence_standard.assessed: Certainty ratings and overall conclusions from systematic reviews or evidence panels (e.g. Campbell, Cochrane, 3ie evidence gap maps, GRADE ratings). Examples are judgements that evidence for a given intervention type is high, moderate, low or very low certainty, or that the evidence is insufficient to rank approaches.
